title: Mangrove forests: guardians of the coast
text:
Along many tropical coasts, there are strange forests that grow with their roots in salty water. These are mangrove forests. Indonesia has more mangrove forest than any other country, and some of it grows along the coasts of Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua.

How mangroves survive

Most plants die in salty water, but mangroves have clever adaptations. Some mangrove trees have roots that stick up out of the mud like straws. These roots take in air, because mud has very little air in it. Other roots are long and arch down from the trunk like stilts, holding the tree upright when the tide rises and falls. Some mangroves can push salt out through their leaves, and white crystals are often seen on the leaves.

A nursery for the sea

The tangled roots make a safe place for young animals. Small fish, shrimp and crabs hide among the roots, where large predators cannot easily reach them. When they grow bigger, many swim out to the open sea. Because of this, mangroves are often called nurseries. Many fish that people eat spend the first part of their lives in mangrove forests.

Protecting the land

Mangroves are also guardians of the coast. Their strong roots hold the mud in place, so the shore does not wash away. The forest also slows down big waves, which helps to protect villages during storms. Scientists have also found that mangroves store a lot of carbon, which helps slow down climate change.

Mangroves in danger

Sadly, in many places mangroves have been cut down to make room for fish ponds, farms and buildings. Some people and schools have started to replant them. A mangrove seedling takes years to become a strong tree, so protecting the trees that are already there is important.

In my opinion, planting a mangrove tree is one of the best things a community can do for its coast.
